I just finished my last year of youth summer theater camp last night and I woke up crying. The end of my camp made me realize: I'm closer to going off to college. I'm close with my parents. Im going to a college nearby though, so that shouldn't be an issue. I'm 18. Never had a job. Never started driving. My parents coddled me and never forced me to "grow up". Also, I'm afraid I won't make friends. Afraid of being expected to be "responsible". Now, I am. But... I have a bad memory which makes it seem like I'm not responsible. In high school, I had terrible teachers who hated me just because I had terrible issues and couldn't come to school sometimes. I'm just scared. I don't even know.

College can be a scary thought. I was very nervous myself. I'd work on the driving thing but don't fret about friends. I'm a loner type myself but even then I managed to get to know a few people. I have several accidental friends now. It just sort of happens. In college your put in positions where working with others is better then not and over time you get to know those people. I wouldn't expect anyone to suddenly change the way they are (I didn't) but it does sort of force you to get to know people. And don't be scared the word forced ether. You won't even notice you are getting to know someone. Whether it's a group project or study group it just happens. College is better then high school despite some harder subjects because you realize your now learning for you instead of going through the motions.

Don't hold your parents accountable for anything. Highschool is a crapshoot at the best of times, but college is the real deal. There is real money going into this and it's the first time you're expected to be an adult. I'm sure you're feeling an immense pressure to succeed. The fact that you're posting on Voat about the fact that you're worried about this proves that you care a whole lot more than people who just barely make it through.

The thing you seem to be worried about is not having a good memory for things. I have a learning disability and it has plagued me on many jobs. I never made mention of it until a manager mentioned that he thought I had one in a private conversation. I acknowledged it then but ignored it for a long time and it was only detrimental. You have to honestly look at your shortcomings (maybe talk to someone close that has worked with you) and find out where the fault lies. I went to a trades school after and actually aced everything I did, because I was more conscious of what I needed to work on. Learning disabilities are all different and just dealing with it is usually terrible advice to give, but at a certain point you have to claim all that you are as what you have to work with, and I think you can get pretty goddamn far if you want to, OP.

Get some routines that involve caring for yourself. Get the right nutrition and get some cardio in. Don't wake up 15 minutes before class, wake up a few hours before to get some good food and even videogame time in. I didn't believe that those two things would help me as much as they did, but it plays into the self-discipline thing,

I haven't gone to college, but I know the stress of starting a new job that I had to move to a new city for. The stress in itself can do you in. I do not deal well with stress and it got the better of me in a few instances. Digging into the routine and dedicating yourself can help, but make sure to observe the people around you. A lot of them are just as scared and stressed out as you are and want a distraction as much as you do.

Also, for the time being really work on getting your drivers licence. Even if you don't have a car, it'll be kind of a studying prep. Go out with a parent and ask them to explain the order of things on the road. This helps on the drivers test a lot.
Self discipline is the real key. I still struggle with this. Start small with little things like I will do 15 push-ups every morning. Then build on it.

I'm thinking of enrolling in a community college next year after I graduate, and then transferring to my local university. I am ridiculed for my plans. However, I think c colleges can give one the financial and mental head start before going to a university.
Voaters who went or are enrolled in a community college, where are you now?

I completed several classes through my local community college in high school. I enjoyed it, and actually a few of the profs I had also taught at several of the local universities that were considerably more expensive. So for those classes I was essentially getting the same education as the students at the private universities for free rather than $800 per credit hour.

The main reason why I didn't complete my first few years at community college before attending a larger four year school was scholarships. All of the scholarships I qualified for at my choice university were only available for first time freshmen, not for transfer students. It would have actually cost me more to do two years at CC and transfer than to do all four years at the school I wanted to attend.

One other potential disadvantage is that not all four year programs will accept all credits from CCs. If you know you want to go on to get your bachelors from a larger university after your time at CC, look into programs you're interested, and figure out what classes will transfer. I had one friend lose almost two full semesters of credits because the program she wanted wouldn't accept many of her classes.

All in all I think that community college can be a great option, as long as you do your research.

You can circumvent the whole credits not transferring by getting your as/aa. No matter what, as long as you have actually that you're good. The university can't argue, they just start you at the classes of your level so you would begin by taking junior level courses.

I started off in community college in 2009. I'm now going to a top ranking university for graduate school in Astronautical Engineering and for work I'm helping design the country's replacement for the shuttle, known as the SLS (space launch system).

My goals are to finish my masters and switch over and work for NASA.

No I do not think there is a disadvantage compared to universities, except for the fact that you may not get the "intro to engineering" type classes you would get if you started off there. otherwise, community college saves quite a bit of money.

I enrolled in CC because my parents did not have the money to send me to university.

Don't let anyone ridicule you for your plans. However, do note that if you end up taking too long at CC or dropping out altogether, you will have given them the idea that they were "right all along" and that you should've listened to them. At the same time, don't think that your classes matter any less than if you would've been at university, because they count just the same (assuming they're transferable courses).

I went to a community college, public university, and private college all within four years, and I can't emphasize the last bit enough. Generally speaking, no one cares about the prestige of the school you went to (and if they do, is that really the kind of environment you want to be in?). I had some of my absolute favorite professors and the community college, and by far encountered the worst ones at the private school. It boils down to the quality of the educators, and how much effort you put into learning the material. If you've got those two things down, it makes it a way better experience.
